text:
Because I knew the names of fish,
even the rarest,
and those of the fishing grounds, and the marks
of distant underwater rocks,
they let me rummage in the baskets,
touch them one by one, weigh them,
and speak openly with me
of the subtle questions of the trade.


Because I understood knots and sails
and how to rig the gear,
they often took me with them;
they gave me a man's work.
I felt with pride
my hands redden at the touch of hemp,
a strong stink of tar and fish
impregnate me.
I knew almost everything of that simple life,
of that daily, primitive chance.


Only that knowledge was luxurious.
They did not know how to tell me,
or I could not understand, what it was like
in the worst days, the bitter
weeks of patience,
when the north wind
gnaws the entrails and the pupil grows tired
of searching the skies,
in the confused days,
when the sea with blurred outlines
is only like a shard of glass
half-buried in mud,
an unpleasant incident or a trap
for those who pass running
blind beneath the rain.

translation.title: Because I Knew the Names of Fish
translation.editorial_note: Translated from the stored Spanish rendering. The speaker's initiation into fishing and the later reversal toward harsh weather and blindness are preserved.
